The valleys of the profile are the intermediates \(B\) and \(C\); the start is \(A\) and the end is \(D\). The data demand four things: \(B\) above \(A\) (\(\Delta H_{i} > 0\)), \(C\) below \(B\) (\(\Delta H_{ii} < 0\)), \(D\) below \(C\) (\(\Delta H_{iii} < 0\)), and \(D\) above \(A\) overall (the reaction \(A \rightarrow D\) is endothermic). Three humps are required because there are three elementary steps.

In graph (A) the final plateau lies above the second valley, so \(\Delta H_{iii}\) would be positive. In graph (B) the second valley lies above the first, so \(\Delta H_{ii}\) would be positive. In graph (D) the first valley falls below the starting level, so \(\Delta H_{i}\) would be negative. Only graph (C) has the first valley above the start, then each successive valley and the final plateau stepping down, while the final level still sits above the initial level. Hence option (C).

Reading the four structures: (I) is a tetrasubstituted alkene (two alkyl groups on each doubly bonded carbon), (II) is trans-2-butene (one alkyl and one H on each carbon, alkyl groups on opposite sides), (III) is a trisubstituted alkene (two alkyl groups on one carbon, one on the other), and (IV) is cis-2-butene (alkyl groups on the same side).

Alkene stability rises with the number of alkyl substituents because of hyperconjugation and the \(+I\) effect, so tetra \(>\) tri \(>\) di. Among the two disubstituted isomers, trans is more stable than cis because the cis isomer suffers steric strain between the two eclipsing methyl groups. Therefore I \(>\) III \(>\) II \(>\) IV, which is option (C).

(A) False. In \(NH_{3}\) the lone-pair moment and the three bond moments point the same way, giving \(\mu \approx 1.47\) D; in \(NF_{3}\) the \(N \rightarrow F\) bond moments oppose the lone-pair moment, so they largely cancel and \(\mu \approx 0.23\) D. \(NF_{3}\) is therefore lower, not higher.

(B) True. \(BeH_{2}\) is \(sp\) hybridised and linear, so the two equal and opposite \(Be-H\) bond moments cancel exactly and \(\mu = 0\).

(C) True. \(O_{2}^{2-}\) has 18 electrons and bond order \(= (10-8)/2 = 1\); \(F_{2}\) also has 18 electrons and bond order 1. The two are equal.

(D) False. In the ozone resonance structure the central oxygen has one lone pair and three bonding pairs, so its formal charge is \(6 - 2 - 3 = +1\), not \(-1\).

(E) False. \(NO_{2}\) has 17 valence electrons; it is an odd-electron species in which nitrogen is left with seven electrons, so the octet is not satisfied and the molecule dimerises to \(N_{2}O_{4}\).

Only B and C are correct, giving option (B).

Reading the four structures: (A) is \(p\)-methoxybenzenediazonium chloride, (B) is \(p\)-nitrobenzenediazonium chloride, (C) is benzenediazonium chloride, and (D) is \(p\)-cyanobenzenediazonium chloride.

The three required behaviours are: \(x\) freely soluble in cold water, \(y\) sparingly soluble in cold water, and \(z\) insoluble in cold water but dissolving on heating.

\(CuCl_{2}\) is a typical freely water-soluble transition metal chloride, so it fits \(x\). \(AgCl\) has a very small solubility product and is the classic sparingly soluble chloride, fitting \(y\). \(PbCl_{2}\) is insoluble in cold water but dissolves appreciably in hot water, which is the standard qualitative-analysis test used to separate lead from silver and mercurous chloride, so it fits \(z\).

Match each name to the structure in which the halogen sits on the characteristic carbon.

(A) Vinyl chloride has chlorine bonded directly to an \(sp^{2}\) carbon of a double bond, i.e. \(CH_{2}=CHCl\), which is (III).

(B) Benzyl chloride has chlorine on the carbon attached to a benzene ring; the figure shows \(C_{6}H_{5}-CH(CH_{3})-Cl\), a benzylic halide, which is (IV).

(C) Alkyl chloride has chlorine on an \(sp^{3}\) carbon of a simple alkyl chain, \(CH_{3}-CH(Cl)-CH_{3}\), which is (II).

(D) Allyl chloride has chlorine on the carbon adjacent to a double bond, \(CH_{2}=CH-CH_{2}Cl\), which is (I).

So A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I, giving option (C).

Relative lowering of vapour pressure for an electrolyte, in the dilute limit, equals the effective mole fraction of the solute particles:

\(\dfrac{p^{\circ}-p}{p^{\circ}} = i\,x_{2} = \dfrac{640-600}{640} = \dfrac{40}{640} = \dfrac{1}{16}\).

The boiling-point elevation fixes \(i\). The molality is \(m = \dfrac{W/M}{0.100\ \mathrm{kg}} = \dfrac{10W}{M}\), since 100 mL of water weighs 100 g. With \(\Delta T_{b} = 375 - 373 = 2\) K,

\(2 = i \times 0.52 \times \dfrac{10W}{M} \Rightarrow i = \dfrac{2M}{5.2\,W}\).

Therefore

\(x_{2} = \dfrac{1}{16i} = \dfrac{1}{16} \times \dfrac{5.2\,W}{2M} = \dfrac{5.2}{32}\cdot\dfrac{W}{M} = \dfrac{1.3}{8}\cdot\dfrac{W}{M}\).

Hence option (A).

For an ideal gas under isothermal conditions:

(A) Reversible expansion. The external pressure matches the gas pressure at every instant, so \(w = -\int p\,dV = -nRT\ln\dfrac{V_{f}}{V_{i}}\), which is (II).

(B) Free expansion. The gas expands into vacuum, \(p_{ex} = 0\), so \(w = 0\), which is (I).

(C) Irreversible expansion. The external pressure is constant, so \(w = -p_{ex}(V_{f}-V_{i})\); since \(V_{f} > V_{i}\) this is negative, as expansion work must be. That is (III).

(D) Irreversible compression. Now the gas is compressed from the larger volume \(V_{f}\) to the smaller \(V_{i}\), so \(w = -p_{ex}(V_{i}-V_{f})\), a positive quantity, as work done on the gas must be. That is (IV).

A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV, giving option (D).

Reading the figure: A is 2-methoxytetrahydrofuran, in which one ring carbon carries both the ring oxygen and an \(-OCH_{3}\) group, i.e. a cyclic acetal. B is 3-methoxytetrahydrofuran, a simple ether. C is 2-hydroxytetrahydrofuran, in which one ring carbon carries both the ring oxygen and an \(-OH\) group, i.e. a cyclic hemiacetal (a lactol). D is 3-hydroxytetrahydrofuran, a simple alcohol.

Only the cyclic hemiacetal is in equilibrium with an open-chain form. Ring opening of C gives 4-hydroxybutanal, which carries a free \(-CHO\) group and is therefore oxidised by Tollens reagent with deposition of a silver mirror. An acetal is locked and does not ring-open under the mildly basic Tollens conditions, and plain ethers and alcohols are unreactive.

The compound is C, which is option (D).

In \(CH_{2}=CH-Cl\) the chlorine is attached to an \(sp^{2}\) carbon and its lone pair is delocalised into the \(\pi\) system, giving the \(C-Cl\) bond partial double-bond character. The greater \(s\) character of the \(sp^{2}\) carbon and this resonance both shorten and strengthen the bond relative to the \(sp^{3}\) \(C-Cl\) bond of \(CH_{3}-CH_{2}-Cl\).

Reading the figure, the five benzylic carbanions are (I) \(p\)-Br, (II) unsubstituted, (III) \(p\)-\(OCH_{3}\), (IV) \(p\)-CHO, (V) \(p\)-\(CH_{3}\).

A carbanion carries a negative charge, so an electron-withdrawing substituent stabilises it and an electron-releasing substituent destabilises it.

\(-CHO\) at the para position is a strong \(-M\) group in direct conjugation with the carbanion, so it delocalises the charge onto the carbonyl oxygen: (IV) is the most stable. \(-Br\) is weakly \(+M\) but dominantly \(-I\), so it is mildly stabilising: (I) comes next, above the unsubstituted (II). \(-CH_{3}\) is \(+I\) and hyperconjugatively electron releasing, so (V) is destabilised below (II). \(-OCH_{3}\) at the para position pushes a lone pair straight onto the carbanion carbon by strong \(+M\), which is the worst possible situation, so (III) is the least stable.

Order: IV \(>\) I \(>\) II \(>\) V \(>\) III, which is option (C).

Statement I is true. Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period. \(K\) is a group-1 element of period 4 and is the most metallic; \(Mg\) is group 2 of period 3; \(Al\) is group 13 of period 3 and so lies to the right of \(Mg\); \(B\) is group 13 of period 2, a metalloid and the least metallic. Hence \(K > Mg > Al > B\) is correct.

Statement II is false. The claim that the atomic radius is always greater than the ionic radius fails for anions: gaining electrons increases inter-electronic repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so an anion is larger than its parent atom, for example \(r(Cl^{-}) > r(Cl)\). The statement holds only for cations.

Statement I true, Statement II false, giving option (D).

Throughout the electrolysis the anode reaction in the acidic solution is water oxidation, \(2H_{2}O \rightarrow O_{2} + 4H^{+} + 4e^{-}\), so oxygen is evolved during both stages and \(n(O_{2}) = n(e^{-})/4\).

Stage 1 — deposition of copper. \(n(Cu) = 0.300/63.54 = 4.72 \times 10^{-3}\) mol, and \(Cu^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow Cu\) requires \(n(e^{-}) = 9.44 \times 10^{-3}\) mol. Oxygen released \(= 9.44 \times 10^{-3}/4 = 2.361 \times 10^{-3}\) mol.

Stage 2 — after the copper is exhausted. \(Q = It = 0.600 \times (28 \times 60) = 1008\) C, so \(n(e^{-}) = 1008/96500 = 1.0446 \times 10^{-2}\) mol. Oxygen released \(= 1.0446 \times 10^{-2}/4 = 2.611 \times 10^{-3}\) mol. (Hydrogen is now discharged at the cathode, but the question asks only about oxygen.)

Total \(n(O_{2}) = 2.361 \times 10^{-3} + 2.611 \times 10^{-3} = 4.972 \times 10^{-3}\) mol.

Volume at STP \(= 4.972 \times 10^{-3} \times 22400 = 111.4\) mL, i.e. 111 mL to the nearest integer.

Within a series the lowest-energy line is the one with the smallest energy gap, i.e. the transition from the level immediately above the series limit.

\(L_{1}\) is therefore the \(n=2 \rightarrow n=1\) transition:

\(E(L_{1}) = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{1^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{2^{2}}\right) = 13.6 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 10.2\) eV.

\(B_{1}\) is the \(n=3 \rightarrow n=2\) transition:

\(E(B_{1}) = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{2^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{3^{2}}\right) = 13.6 \times \dfrac{5}{36} = 1.889\) eV.

Hence

\(x = \dfrac{E(L_{1})}{E(B_{1})} = \dfrac{13.6 \times 3/4}{13.6 \times 5/36} = \dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{36}{5} = \dfrac{27}{5} = 5.4\).

Since the answer is required as \(x \times 10^{-1}\), the value entered is 54.

Acidified dichromate is reduced by six electrons per formula unit:

\(Cr_{2}O_{7}^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Cr^{3+} + 7H_{2}O\).

Since the electrons lost in the oxidation half must equal the six electrons gained, each balanced reaction transfers six electrons.

For iodide, \(2I^{-} \rightarrow I_{2} + 2e^{-}\); scaled to the dichromate half-reaction, \(6I^{-} \rightarrow 3I_{2} + 6e^{-}\), so \(X = 6\).

For sulphide, \(S^{2-} \rightarrow S + 2e^{-}\); scaled likewise, \(3S^{2-} \rightarrow 3S + 6e^{-}\), so \(Y = 6\).

Therefore \(X + Y = 6 + 6 = 12\).
